prompt.context: Blue Ivy Airlines is a low-cost, national airline with an emphasis on customer service. Unlike all of its competitors, Blue Ivy currently does not charge passengers for checked bags. The company has experienced decreasing profitability compared to competitors since competitors adopted bag fees. Blue Ivy's primary goal is to increase revenue (costs are largely fixed, making revenue a reasonable proxy for profitability); its secondary goal is to preserve market share on a customers-per-year basis.
prompt.question: Blue Ivy Airlines is considering charging for bags. Is this a good idea?

clarifying_info.q: What is Blue Ivy's business model?
clarifying_info.a: It is a low-cost, national airline with an emphasis on customer service.
Yes, all of Blue Ivy's competitors charge for bag fees.

clarifying_info.q: What is Blue Ivy's primary goal?
clarifying_info.a: To increase revenue. Costs are largely fixed so revenue is a reasonable proxy for profitability. Their secondary goal is preserving market share on a customers/year basis.

clarifying_info.q: Why is Blue Ivy considering this?
clarifying_info.a: Blue Ivy has experienced decreasing profitability compared to competitors since competitors adopted this strategy.

framework: Revenue impact: Quantify incremental bag-fee revenue vs. ticket revenue lost from customer attrition — run a breakeven analysis
Bag fee revenue = Bag Fee × % checking × Avg Flight Capacity × Flights per aircraft per day × Fleet size
Lost ticket revenue = Avg Ticket Price × Customers per day × % customers lost
Customer behavior: Will customers avoid checking bags to avoid fees, leading to overhead bin crowding, delayed takeoffs, increased gate/flight attendant costs, and lower satisfaction?
Customer satisfaction and brand equity: Damage to brand image from reversing a differentiating policy
Competitive dynamics: Will a competitor fill the 'free bags' niche Blue Ivy vacates? Are competitors who charge for bags gaining or sacrificing revenue for market share?
Market positioning: Blue Ivy currently holds a unique moat as the only carrier not charging for bags; abandoning this may invite new entrants into that niche

questions.prompt: Perform a breakeven / revenue impact analysis: will bag fee revenue exceed the revenue lost from customers who switch away?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the two offsetting revenue streams and set up the math for each. Strong candidates will recognize this as a breakeven problem and work through both sides before drawing a conclusion.

math.setup: Bag Revenue per day = Bag Fee × % checking × Avg Flight Capacity × Flights per aircraft per day × Fleet Size; Lost Revenue per day = Avg Ticket Price × Customers per day × % lost
steps: Total customers per day = 150 seats × 4 flights/aircraft/day × 150 aircraft = 90,000
math.answer: Charging for bags results in a net revenue loss of approximately $90,000 per day (~$33M per year) because lost ticket revenue ($990K/day) exceeds incremental bag fee revenue ($900K/day).

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the quantitative revenue impact, what qualitative and strategic factors should Blue Ivy consider when deciding whether to charge for bags?

categories.name: Brand and customer experience
ideas: Damage to brand equity built around 'bags fly free' positioning
Increased boarding time as passengers stuff carry-ons to avoid fees
Higher costs for gate agents and flight attendants managing overhead bins

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Blue Ivy currently occupies a unique differentiating niche; charging removes it
A new low-cost entrant could capture the 'no bag fee' positioning Blue Ivy abandons
Competitors who adopted fees may be sacrificing revenue for market share
Need to assess whether competitor revenue grew or shrunk post-adoption

categories.name: Customer segmentation
ideas: Families likely to check bags regardless — high price sensitivity to fees
Business travelers may be more flexible and willing to pay or carry on
Loyalty program members may respond differently
Opportunity to set lower ticket prices to offset fee impact for price-sensitive segments

categories.name: Longer-term revenue trajectory
ideas: Short-term customer loss may be temporary if industry norm shifts
Long-term: will customers adjust behavior and accept fees?
Consumer price sensitivity analysis — could a lower fee retain more passengers?
Research into elasticity of demand at various fee levels

recommendation: The data favor NOT charging for bags: initial analysis shows bag fees will reduce net revenue by ~$33M annually because lost ticket revenue exceeds incremental bag fee revenue
Blue Ivy's 'no bag fee' policy is a meaningful competitive moat; abandoning it cedes a differentiating position and invites competitors to occupy that niche
If the client still considers launching, it should combine bag fees with lower base ticket prices and treat the first 12 months as a controlled experiment with close monitoring of customer retention
Either recommendation (charge or do not charge) is acceptable if the candidate addresses: (i) short-term revenue loss, (ii) brand/reputation risk, and (iii) loss of competitive moat
risks: If Blue Ivy does NOT charge: continued relative revenue and market-share erosion as all competitors benefit from ancillary fee revenue
If Blue Ivy DOES charge: permanent loss of core customer base loyal to the 'bags fly free' brand; risk of a new entrant capturing vacated niche
Competitors may be sacrificing revenue for market share in the short run — Blue Ivy may be winning on profitability even while losing on passenger count
next_steps: Customer segment analysis: determine whether the projected 11% churn is concentrated in price-sensitive or loyalty segments, and whether loss is temporary or permanent
Competitive intelligence: assess whether competitors' revenues grew or shrank after adopting bag fees
Consumer price-sensitivity research: test lower fee levels (e.g., $15) to find a price point that retains more passengers while still generating net positive revenue
Long-term revenue modeling: build a multi-year forecast that accounts for potential customer re-adjustment and competitor response
Brand impact study: survey current customers on likelihood to switch if fees are introduced
